CausalChain: Hypoxia -> HIF activation -> Upregulation of glycolytic enzymes (HK2, LDHA) -> Elevated lactate production -> Acidification of tumor microenvironment -> Lactate receptor (GPR81) engagement and CA12 upregulation -> M2 macrophage polarization -> Secretion of cytokines (IL-10, TGF-β) and chemokines (CCL8) -> Paracrine induction of PHGDH and serine synthesis in tumor cells -> Increased NADPH production -> Enhanced redox homeostasis -> Therapy resistance to TKIs/ICIs
Hypothesis: Under hypoxic conditions in HCC, HIF-driven metabolic reprogramming increases lactate production, which acidifies the tumor microenvironment. This acidification cooperates with lactate receptor engagement (predominantly via GPR81) to induce TAM polarization towards an M2 phenotype. Simultaneously, the acidic milieu promotes the upregulation of CA12 in macrophages, aiding their survival and enhancing secretion of pro-tumorigenic chemokines such as CCL8. The M2 macrophages secrete specific cytokines—including IL-10 and TGF-β—that act in a paracrine manner on tumor cells to upregulate the serine synthesis pathway through PHGDH induction. The resultant increase in serine metabolism bolsters NADPH production, thereby sustaining redox homeostasis and rendering cancer cells resistant to targeted therapies like TKIs and ICIs. Recognizing that additional metabolic pathways such as AMPK-mediated autophagy may operate concurrently, we aim to leverage advanced tools—such as single-cell RNA-seq, spatial metabolomics, multiplex cytokine profiling, and CRISPR screening—to dissect these interrelated mechanisms and identify precise intervention points to overcome therapy resistance.
Abstract: In hypoxic hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), HIF-mediated metabolic reprogramming not only stimulates glycolysis and lactate production but also orchestrates a multifaceted interplay between tumor cells and the tumor microenvironment. Our refined hypothesis posits that excess lactate acidifies the microenvironment and, through specific receptor engagement (including GPR81), drives the polarization of tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) toward an M2 phenotype. This polarization is further reinforced by an adaptive surge in carbonic anhydrase XII (CA12) in macrophages, which facilitates survival under acidic conditions and supports chemokine secretion (e.g., CCL8). These infiltrating M2 macrophages secrete cytokines—most notably IL-10 and TGF-β—that, acting in a paracrine fashion, upregulate the serine synthesis pathway via PHGDH induction in cancer cells. The enhanced serine metabolism increases NADPH production, thereby strengthening redox homeostasis and contributing to resistance against tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) and immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). This study will employ contemporary technologies including single-cell RNA sequencing, spatial metabolomics, multiplex cytokine profiling, and CRISPR screens to unravel and target the multiple intercellular signaling routes that converge on therapy resistance.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis highlighted a HIF-driven lactate production leading to M2 polarization with a paracrine induction of serine synthesis in cancer cells via PHGDH, bolstering NADPH production and resistance. The revised hypothesis retains these core elements but incorporates additional observations: (1) It explicitly acknowledges the role of CA12 upregulation in macrophages as an adaptive response to acidification, which supports TAM survival and facilitates chemokine secretion (e.g., CCL8) associated with epithelial-mesenchymal transition. (2) It recognizes the possibility of parallel metabolic reprogramming through alternative pathways such as AMPK signaling and autophagy. (3) It broadens the methodological approach to include multiplex cytokine profiling alongside single-cell RNA sequencing, spatial metabolomics, and CRISPR screens. These revisions ensure a more comprehensive and testable model that integrates both the original causal chain and novel, contextually supported mechanisms.
